props.sub: four more behavioral questions · with full worked answers · Senior EM

props.title: Leading a remote or distributed team
props.q: How do you lead a remote or globally distributed team?

moves.title: Default to written and async
moves.desc: Docs and clear decisions over meetings. Timezone-fair, not meeting-heavy.

moves.title: Engineer connection on purpose
moves.desc: Trust doesn't happen by accident remotely. Create the moments deliberately.

moves.title: Measure outcomes, not presence
moves.desc: Judge output and impact, never hours online or the green dot.

moves.title: Over-communicate context
moves.desc: Remote teams starve on missing context. You feed it relentlessly.

props.trap: You recreated the office online — back-to-back calls across incompatible timezones.
props.signal: You build trust and clarity across distance, and treat async as a feature, not a compromise.
props.foot: Remote leadership is a discipline: written clarity, deliberate connection, outcomes over optics.

props.title: Building one team across three continents
props.situation: I inherited a team split across San Francisco, London, and Bangalore — a fourteen-hour spread. In reality it was three sub-teams that didn't trust each other; meetings excluded someone by design, and context lived in people's heads.
props.task: My mandate: turn three timezones into one team, without burning anyone out on 2am calls.

actions.d: Moved decisions to writing — every significant decision landed in a doc, so nobody was excluded by their timezone.
Rotated the pain fairly — the one necessary sync meeting rotated its awkward hour, so it wasn't always Bangalore's midnight.
Engineered connection deliberately — regional leads, cross-site pairing, and real budget for periodic in-person weeks.
Judged outcomes, not presence — I killed the green-dot culture and measured shipped impact instead.

props.learning: Distributed teams run on written clarity and deliberate trust, not on more meetings.
props.foot: You made distance a design constraint you solved, not an excuse. That's modern EM leadership.

props.title: Building an inclusive team in practice
props.q: What have you actually done to build a diverse, inclusive team?

moves.title: Move past slogans to actions
moves.desc: Talk about what you changed in hiring and daily practice, not your values.

moves.title: Fix the system, not the people
moves.desc: Structured interviews, diverse panels, wider sourcing — take bias out of the process.

moves.title: Make inclusion a daily practice
moves.desc: Airtime in meetings, credit attribution, equitable stretch work and on-call.

moves.title: Hold yourself to data
moves.desc: Track representation, promotion rates, and who gets the good projects.

props.trap: You gave a values speech with no concrete action or measurement behind it.
props.signal: You treat inclusion as an operational discipline with real interventions and metrics.
props.foot: Inclusion isn't a poster. It's who you hire, who speaks, who gets the growth work, and who gets promoted.

props.title: The team where only some voices got heard
props.situation: I took over a team that, on paper, looked fairly diverse. But the same three senior men made every real decision, and our quieter engineers and women were leaving faster than anyone else.
props.task: My mandate: turn nominal diversity into real inclusion, and stop the lopsided attrition.

actions.d: Looked at the data first — the growth projects and the promotions were all going to the same few people.
Changed the meeting mechanics — round-robin input, written proposals before discussion, and I attributed ideas to their real authors.
Redistributed the good work — rotated high-visibility projects and on-call, so growth wasn't reserved for the loudest.
Fixed hiring too — diverse interview panels and a structured rubric, so the funnel genuinely widened.

props.learning: Diversity is who's in the room. Inclusion is who actually gets heard, grown, and promoted.
props.foot: You made inclusion measurable and operational, not a slogan. That's what interviewers respect.

props.title: Building a healthy on-call & reliability culture
props.q: How do you build a sustainable on-call and reliability culture?

moves.title: Treat toil as a bug
moves.desc: A brutal on-call is a systems failure, not a rite of passage. Own it.

moves.title: Make reliability visible and funded
moves.desc: SLOs and error budgets, with real time allocated to pay down toil.

moves.title: Blameless by default
moves.desc: Postmortems find system fixes, not scapegoats — or people stop reporting.

moves.title: Protect the humans
moves.desc: Fair rotation, comp for pages, hard caps. Burnout is a reliability risk too.

props.trap: You treated a painful on-call as normal, and let your best people burn out on it.
props.signal: You build reliability as a system and a culture, and you protect the people running it.
props.foot: Reliability is a culture: SLOs, blameless learning, and humane rotations — not heroics.

props.title: The on-call rotation that was burning people out
props.situation: I took over a team with a brutal on-call. Engineers were getting paged around twenty times a week, mostly for noise. Two people had already quit citing burnout, and everyone dreaded their week on rotation.
props.task: My mandate: make on-call sustainable, without letting reliability actually get worse.

actions.d: Treated the toil as a bug — I had the team spend twenty percent of every sprint killing the top sources of alerts.
Made reliability visible — introduced SLOs and an error budget, so reliability work got real, funded priority.
Went fully blameless — rewrote postmortems to hunt system fixes, never people, so incidents got surfaced, not hidden.
Protected the humans — fair rotation, follow-the-sun where possible, and a hard rule: a bad night earns the next day off.

props.learning: A painful on-call is a systems failure. Fix the toil, fund reliability, and protect the people.
props.foot: You turned a burnout machine into a healthy system. That's operational leadership, not heroics.

props.title: Setting technical strategy across teams
props.q: Tell me about a time you set technical strategy beyond your team.

moves.title: Start from the business goal
moves.desc: Strategy connects tech investment to where the business is going, not to a favorite rewrite.

moves.title: Get the org bought in
moves.desc: Write it down, socialize it, and let stakeholders shape it so they own it.

moves.title: Sequence bets, and say no
moves.desc: A roadmap is mostly what you WON'T do. Make the trade-offs explicit.

moves.title: Make it real and measurable
moves.desc: Tie it to milestones and metrics, and revisit it. A static strategy is a wish.

props.trap: You proposed a grand rewrite with no link to business value and no buy-in.
props.signal: You think in bets and trade-offs at the org level, and can align people behind a direction.
props.foot: A technical strategy is funded bets tied to business outcomes — and the things you chose NOT to do.

props.title: A three-year platform strategy nobody had written
props.situation: Across our engineering org of eighty people, every team was independently reinventing infrastructure — auth, data pipelines, deploy tooling. There was no shared platform strategy, and it was quietly costing us a fortune in duplicated effort and incidents.
props.task: My mandate — I raised my hand for it: write and drive a shared platform strategy for the whole org.

actions.d: Started from the business goal — I tied the strategy to shipping faster and cheaper, not to elegant architecture.
Built it WITH the org, not for it — interviewed every team lead, wrote a one-page strategy, and let them shape it so they'd own it.
Made it a sequence of bets — I named what we'd build, what we'd buy, and what we'd deliberately NOT do, staged over three phases.
Made it measurable — every bet had a milestone and a metric, and we revisited the whole strategy each quarter.

props.learning: Strategy is funded bets tied to business outcomes — and the courage to write down what you won't do.
props.foot: You aligned a whole org behind a direction and made the trade-offs explicit. The senior-EM ceiling.

items: Lead remote teams with written clarity and deliberate trust.
Make inclusion operational: who's heard, grown, and promoted.
Build reliability as a culture, and protect your on-call people.
Strategy is funded bets tied to business outcomes.
Across all four parts: STAR, plus what you learned.
props.closer: Great managers build systems and cultures that outlast them.
